1	=== PAGE 1 ===
2	530571PSSXXX10.1177/0956797614530571Maglio, PolmanOrientation and Distance
3	research-article2014
4	Research Article
5	Spatial Orientation Shrinks and Expands
6	Psychological Distance
7	Psychological Science
8	2014, Vol. 25(7) 1345­ –1352
9	© The Author(s) 2014
10	Reprints and permissions:
11	sagepub.com/journalsPermissions.nav
12	DOI: 10.1177/0956797614530571
13	pss.sagepub.com
14	Sam J. Maglio1 and Evan Polman2
15	1Department of Marketing, University of Toronto Scarborough, and 2Department of Marketing,
16	University of Wisconsin–Madison
17	Abstract
18	Being objectively close to or far from a place changes how people perceive the location of that place in a subjective,
19	psychological sense. In the six studies reported here, we investigated whether people’s spatial orientation (defined as
20	moving toward or away from a place) will produce similar effects—by specifically influencing psychological closeness
21	in each of its forms (i.e., spatial, temporal, probabilistic, and social distance). Orientation influenced subjective spatial
22	distance at various levels of objective distance (Study 1), regardless of the direction people were facing (Study 2). In
23	addition, when spatially oriented toward, rather than away from, a particular place, participants felt that events there
24	had occurred more recently (Studies 3a and 3b) and that events there would be more likely to occur (Study 4). Finally,
25	participants felt more similarity to people who were spatially oriented toward them than to people who were spatially
26	oriented away from them (Study 5). Our investigation broadens the study of psychological distance from static spatial
27	locations to dynamically moving points in space.
28	Keywords
29	psychological distance, space, motion, distance perception, open data, open materials
30	Received 1/22/14; Revision accepted 3/10/14
31	Americans, on average, take 5,117 steps a day (Bassett,
32	Wyatt, Thompson, Peters, & Hill, 2010) and drive more than
33	14,000 miles a year (U.S. Department of Transportation,
34	2011). Mounting research on the psychology of spatial
35	distance has articulated the many ways in which feeling
36	closer to or farther from things changes the manner in
37	which people represent and act on those very things
38	(e.g., Trope & Liberman, 2010). Spatial distance has the
39	power to shape judgments, yet most researchers who
40	have studied spatial distance have adopted primarily a
41	static or binary approach, conceptualizing objects as sta-
42	tionary, either near or far in space (Henderson & Wakslak,
43	2010). In the current research, we went a step further by
44	considering the dynamic and changeable orientation of
45	people who are moving toward or away from objects in
46	their environment. We hypothesized that feelings of
47	closeness are shaped not only by spatial distance, but
48	also by people’s orientation in space—that is, their move-
49	ment toward or away from places, people, and things.
50	By analogy, one can view spatial orientation as a vec-
51	tor—a term used in physics to describe a quantity that
52	has both magnitude (e.g., 1 mile) and direction (e.g.,
53	westward). In contrast, research in psychology to date
54	has viewed distance predominantly as a scalar—a quan-
55	tity that has a changeable magnitude but constant direc-
56	tion. In other words, past research has assumed that
57	direction is inexorably linked with magnitude. However,
58	this does not have to be the case: One can be equally
59	distant from two different locations, but the direction one
60	pursues to one location can be different from the direc-
61	tion one pursues to the other location. This is an example
62	of orientation, or the direction in which a person is head-
63	ing relative to a target object.
64	To be sure, past research has identified the effects of
65	changing orientation on judgments of spatial distance.
66	For instance, leaning toward (vs. away from) a computer
67	monitor causes people to feel that the monitor is closer
68	(and stimuli presented on the monitor are evaluated
69	accordingly; Thomas & Tsai, 2012), and stepping toward
70	Corresponding Author:
71	Sam J. Maglio, University of Toronto Scarborough–Management, 1265
72	Military Trail, Toronto, Ontario M1C 1A4, Canada
73	E-mail: sam.maglio@utoronto.ca
74	=== PAGE 2 ===
75	1346 Maglio, Polman
76	(vs. away from) something causes people to treat that
77	object as if it were closer (Koch, Holland, Hengstler, &
78	van Knippenberg, 2009). We hasten to note that these
79	findings, however, relied on changes in both orientation
80	and distance, in which changes to orientation (e.g., step-
81	ping forward) also entailed changes to objective distance
82	(e.g., being closer). In the studies reported here, we went
83	beyond past research by holding objective distance con-
84	stant and considering only the orientation of the person
85	relative to the target object (and vice versa). We predicted
86	that people will feel closer to a target when they are ori-
87	ented toward it than when they are oriented away from it
88	despite maintaining a constant objective distance.
89	To investigate this possibility, we conceptualized phys-
90	ical space as but one type of psychological distance
91	(Liberman, Trope, & Stephan, 2007; Trope & Liberman,
92	2010). This broader construct encapsulates four dimen-
93	sions along which targets can vary in their closeness to
94	the individual: spatial, temporal, probabilistic, and social.
95	People feel more distant from places when those places
96	are further away in physical space and feel more distant
97	from times when those times are from the past or future
98	rather than the present. In addition, unlikely events feel
99	more distant than likely events, and people who are per-
100	ceived as dissimilar to the self feel more distant than peo-
101	ple who are perceived as similar. Adopting this perspective
102	affords consideration of orientation that is more broadly
103	defined. With respect to time, people feel that future
104	events are subjectively closer than past events, even
105	when the objective temporal distance is held constant
106	(Caruso, Van Boven, Chin, & Ward, 2013). In the social
107	dimension, Smith and Trope (2006) identified power as
108	one aspect of social distance, and people confer more
109	status to employees who move upward, rather than
110	downward, in a status hierarchy, even when the employ-
111	ees’ ultimate rank in the hierarchy is held constant (Pettit,
112	Sivanathan, Gladstone, & Carson Marr, 2013).
113	Viewed from the perspective of psychological distance
114	as a broader, multidimensional construct, the closeness
115	we predicted to be engendered by spatial orientation
116	takes on a unique meaning. Despite differences among
117	the four dimensions of distance, they are all avenues of
118	removal from immediate experience in the here and now
119	(Maglio, Trope, & Liberman, 2013). As a result, people
120	extrapolate from information about a target’s location
121	along one avenue of psychological distance (i.e., physical
122	proximity) to infer its location on all avenues (i.e., tem-
123	poral, probabilistic, and social proximity). That is, if a
124	place, person, or event feels psychologically close in one
125	way, then it feels close in all ways (Bar-Anan, Liberman,
126	Trope, & Algom, 2007; Fiedler, Jung, Wänke, &
127	Alexopoulos, 2012; Van Boven, Kane, McGraw, & Dale,
128	2010). This shared meaning is further supported by
129	explicit judgments across different dimensions.
130	Building from such cross-dimensional accounts, we
131	reasoned that if spatial orientation toward a place, per-
132	son, or event causes it to feel closer in physical space, it
133	should cause similar feelings of closeness on each of the
134	other three dimensions of distance as well. The following
135	studies tested this account. For each study, we decided
136	ahead of time on a minimum sample size per cell and
137	collected data until that number was achieved. In all but
138	one of our studies, we chose 20 participants per cell as a
139	minimum on the basis of prior research on psychological
140	distance (and experimental psychology more generally).
141	Study 3a was the first in which we extrapolated from
142	physical space to a different, nonspatial dimension of dis-
143	tance, so we targeted a larger minimum sample of 50
144	participants per cell, because we were unsure of the size
145	of any effect we might observe.
146	Study 1
147	Method
148	Study 1 served two purposes. First, it tested the hypoth-
149	esis that a spatial orientation toward (vs. away from) a
150	location will cause that location to feel closer. Second, it
151	examined the relative contributions of spatial orientation
152	and objective distance as simultaneous yet independent
153	inputs into subjective distance estimates.
154	Two hundred two volunteers were recruited at the Bay
155	Street subway station in Toronto, Ontario, Canada. People

distance at various levels of objective distance (Study 1), regardless of the direction people were facing (Study 2). In

oriented away from them (Study 5). Our investigation broadens the study of psychological distance from static spatial

Americans, on average, take 5,117 steps a day (Bassett,
Wyatt, Thompson, Peters, & Hill, 2010) and drive more than
14,000 miles a year (U.S. Department of Transportation,
2011). Mounting research on the psychology of spatial
distance has articulated the many ways in which feeling
closer to or farther from things changes the manner in
which people represent and act on those very things
(e.g., Trope & Liberman, 2010). Spatial distance has the
power to shape judgments, yet most researchers who
have studied spatial distance have adopted primarily a
static or binary approach, conceptualizing objects as sta-
tionary, either near or far in space (Henderson & Wakslak,
2010). In the current research, we went a step further by
considering the dynamic and changeable orientation of
people who are moving toward or away from objects in
their environment. We hypothesized that feelings of
closeness are shaped not only by spatial distance, but
also by people’s orientation in space—that is, their move-
ment toward or away from places, people, and things.
By analogy, one can view spatial orientation as a vec-
tor—a term used in physics to describe a quantity that
has both magnitude (e.g., 1 mile) and direction (e.g.,
westward). In contrast, research in psychology to date
has viewed distance predominantly as a scalar—a quan-
tity that has a changeable magnitude but constant direc-
tion. In other words, past research has assumed that
direction is inexorably linked with magnitude. However,
this does not have to be the case: One can be equally
distant from two different locations, but the direction one
pursues to one location can be different from the direc-
tion one pursues to the other location. This is an example
of orientation, or the direction in which a person is head-
ing relative to a target object.
To be sure, past research has identified the effects of
changing orientation on judgments of spatial distance.

relative to the target object (and vice versa). We predicted
that people will feel closer to a target when they are ori-

despite maintaining a constant objective distance.

(Liberman, Trope, & Stephan, 2007; Trope & Liberman,
2010). This broader construct encapsulates four dimen-
sions along which targets can vary in their closeness to
the individual: spatial, temporal, probabilistic, and social.

are further away in physical space and feel more distant
from times when those times are from the past or future
rather than the present. In addition, unlikely events feel
more distant than likely events, and people who are per-

affords consideration of orientation that is more broadly
defined. With respect to time, people feel that future

# Partial eta squared from a car::Anova table
add_pes <- function(tab) {
  ss_err <- tab["Residuals", "Sum Sq"]
  tab |>
    as.data.frame() |>
    rownames_to_column("term") |>
    filter(!term %in% c("(Intercept)", "Residuals")) |>
    transmute(term, df1 = Df, df2 = tab["Residuals", "Df"],
              F = `F value`, p = `Pr(>F)`, pes = `Sum Sq` / (`Sum Sq` + ss_err))
}

# --- Omnibus 2 x 4 between-subjects ANOVA ---------------------------------
# Cells are unequal (23-26), so the SS type matters. Type III with sum-to-zero

m_dir <- lm(DISTANCE ~ direction * station, data = d,

55: ```{r}
56: #| label: setup
57: library(tidyverse)
58: library(readxl) # read the authors' .xlsx file
59: library(car)    # Type III sums of squares (SPSS-style), via car::Anova()
60: library(knitr)  # tables
63: ```{r}
64: #| label: load
65: d_raw <- read_excel("partA/data/S1_Subway.xlsx")
67: glimpse(d_raw)
68: count(d_raw, DIRECTION)                       # paper: n = 101 per platform
69: count(d_raw, STN_NUMBER, STN_NAME, DIRECTION) # cell sizes
72: ```{r}
73: #| label: preprocess
74: station_labels <- c(SPAD = "Spadina", STG = "St. George",
75:                     `B-Y` = "Bloor-Yonge", SHER = "Sherbourne")
77: d <- d_raw |>
78:   mutate(
79:     # stations ordered west to east, as in the paper and STN_NUMBER
80:     station   = factor(station_labels[STN_NAME], levels = station_labels),
81:     direction = factor(str_to_title(DIRECTION), levels = c("East", "West")),
82:     side      = if_else(station %in% c("Spadina", "St. George"), "West of Bay", "East of Bay"),
83:     # literal toward/away coding: heading east is toward the two east stations
84:     orientation = factor(
85:       if_else((direction == "East" & side == "East of Bay") |
86:               (direction == "West" & side == "West of Bay"), "Toward", "Away"),
87:       levels = c("Toward", "Away"))
88:   )
90: stopifnot(nrow(d) == 202, !anyNA(d$station), !anyNA(d$DISTANCE))
92: cell_stats <- d |>
93:   group_by(station, direction) |>
94:   summarise(n = n(), mean = mean(DISTANCE), sd = sd(DISTANCE),
95:             se = sd / sqrt(n), .groups = "drop")
96: kable(cell_stats, digits = 2)
99: ```{r}
100: #| label: fig1
101: #| fig-cap: "Reproduction of Figure 1: mean subjective distance (±1 SE) by station and travel direction."
102: ggplot(cell_stats, aes(station, mean, fill = direction)) +
103:   geom_col(position = position_dodge(0.8), width = 0.75) +
104:   geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean - se, ymax = mean + se),
105:                 position = position_dodge(0.8), width = 0.2) +
106:   scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 5), breaks = seq(0, 5, 0.5)) +
107:   scale_fill_manual(values = c(East = "grey30", West = "grey75"),
108:                     labels = c(East = "Traveling East", West = "Traveling West")) +
109:   labs(x = NULL, y = "Subjective Distance", fill = NULL) +
110:   theme_classic() +
111:   theme(legend.position = "top")
114: ```{r}
115: #| label: analysis
116: # Partial eta squared from a car::Anova table
117: add_pes <- function(tab) {
118:   ss_err <- tab["Residuals", "Sum Sq"]
119:   tab |>
120:     as.data.frame() |>
121:     rownames_to_column("term") |>
122:     filter(!term %in% c("(Intercept)", "Residuals")) |>
123:     transmute(term, df1 = Df, df2 = tab["Residuals", "Df"],
124:               F = `F value`, p = `Pr(>F)`, pes = `Sum Sq` / (`Sum Sq` + ss_err))
125: }
127: # --- Omnibus 2 x 4 between-subjects ANOVA ---------------------------------
128: # Cells are unequal (23-26), so the SS type matters. Type III with sum-to-zero
129: # contrasts (SPSS's default) is used here.
130: #
131: # The between-subjects factor that reproduces the paper is travel DIRECTION
132: # (eastbound vs. westbound platform). The paper labels this factor
133: # "orientation", but within a station, direction is exactly what varies.
134: m_dir <- lm(DISTANCE ~ direction * station, data = d,
135:             contrasts = list(direction = contr.sum, station = contr.sum))
136: omnibus <- add_pes(Anova(m_dir, type = 3))
137: kable(omnibus, digits = 3, caption = "Type III ANOVA: direction × station")
139: # For comparison: other SS types for the same model
140: kable(add_pes(Anova(m_dir, type = 2)), digits = 3, caption = "Type II (same model)")
141: kable(anova(m_dir) |> as.data.frame() |> rownames_to_column("term"),
142:       digits = 3, caption = "Type I / sequential (same model)")
144: # For comparison: literal toward/away coding of orientation. This model gives
145: # a large orientation main effect and no interaction, the reverse of what the
146: # paper reports, so it is not what the authors ran.
147: m_orient <- lm(DISTANCE ~ orientation * station, data = d,
148:                contrasts = list(orientation = contr.sum, station = contr.sum))
149: kable(add_pes(Anova(m_orient, type = 3)), digits = 3,
150:       caption = "Type III ANOVA with literal toward/away coding (not the paper's analysis)")
152: # --- Station-specific comparisons (East vs. West) --------------------------
153: # A separate one-way ANOVA (= pooled-variance t test) within each station.
154: # ηp² = SS_direction / (SS_direction + SS_error) within that station.
155: simple_effects <- d |>
156:   group_by(station) |>
157:   group_modify(\(ds, key) {
158:     a <- anova(lm(DISTANCE ~ direction, data = ds))
159:     tibble(mean_east = mean(ds$DISTANCE[ds$direction == "East"]),

I'm done with Part A, and I think it succeeded: all seven target outcomes from Study 1 come out the same as the paper at the precision it reports. The code is in [partA.qmd](partA.qmd) and renders without errors to `partA.html`.

There's no analysis code, so I had to work out three of the authors' choices. Each one is shown in the file next to the alternatives:

- **What "orientation" means in the ANOVA:** The paper calls the factor "orientation (toward, away from)", but its numbers only come out if the factor is **travel direction** (eastbound vs. westbound). If you code toward/away literally, you get the opposite result: a large orientation main effect (F = 46.0) and no interaction (F = 0.93). This doesn't change the conclusion, but the paper's wording doesn't match what was actually run. It's probably the most important thing to note in your verdict.
- **Type of sums of squares:** The cell sizes are unequal (23–26), and only Type III gives station F = 24.10. Types I and II give 23.35. Type III is SPSS's default, which is probably what they used.
- **Station-level tests:** These are separate one-way ANOVAs within each station. Testing them against the omnibus error term instead gives Bloor-Yonge p = .051 rather than .053.

The data had no exclusions or cleaning steps. The file matches the paper's N = 202 (101 per platform).
